verses.translation_literal: Hallelu-Yah! Praise [obj] YHWH from the heavens; praise him in the heights.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise Yah! Let the LORD be praised — and let it begin on high, from the heavens, from the far heights where no voice of earth has ever climbed. Praise him there.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a shout and then an address: everyone is told to praise, and 'from the heavens' says where the praise starts, not who is being asked. The first speakers are the ones nearest the throne. Hebrew writes the opening cry as two words, 'praise' and 'Yah' (a short form of the divine name), and the actor should take the second word as a name, not a stock phrase.

The KJV folds the cry into a single 'Praise ye the Lord', which loses the doubled imperative: three times in this verse and the next the verb 'praise' is hurled, each time to a wider crowd. Note also that the KJV replaces YHWH with 'the Lord' in both clauses, though the verse says Yah and then YHWH. The psalm is built on one repeated verb (הָלַל), so the actor never gets a break from the beat.

The Targum glosses the heavens' praisers as angelic 'holy creatures', and Ibn Ezra reads the verse as opening on the upper world before turning to the lower; for the stage, simply feel the downward sweep that begins here: heights, then sky, then earth.

philological_notes.note: Plural imperative of the verb 'to praise' (to boast of, to celebrate loudly); the English 'hallelujah' is this word plus 'Yah'. Here it is a command to a whole crowd, repeated three times in one verse.
'From the heavens': Metzudat David reads it as the place the sound of praise comes from. The preposition marks the origin of the praise, not only the people addressed.

verses.translation_literal: Praise him, all his messengers; praise him, all his hosts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him, all you who carry his word; praise him, every one of his hosts, drawn up rank on rank before him.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Messengers' (מַלְאָכִים) is simply what the Hebrew word means; 'angel' is the Greek-derived English habit, and the KJV uses it here as elsewhere. The word names a function, one who is sent. The second line, 'his hosts' (צְבָאָיו), is the language of an army mustered for service, and in the older poetry it can also point to the lights of the sky (the next verse goes on to the sun, moon and stars). So the two lines may be one group seen twice, as a court and as a force.

As a pair of parallel lines, the actors should not play two separate choirs. Both lines are an order given to attendants of a king: a ruler in the ancient Near East was announced by his messengers and surrounded by his troops. Everyone listed so far is in his service, and the psalm is about to extend that service to the sea monsters.

The KJV's 'ye' and 'angels' are fine, but the plain 'messengers' keeps the line from sounding like a Christmas card.

philological_notes.note: 'His messengers', from the verb root for sending. The word names the role, not a species; context decides whether the sender's envoys are human or heavenly.
'His hosts': a military word (army, mustered service). Radak and Meiri read it as the heavenly bodies; Targum reads it as his heavenly troops. The word is Qere here (Ketiv noted in the packet).

verses.translation_literal: Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars of light.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him, sun and moon — you who rule the day and the night; praise him, every star that shines.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the world of the psalmist's neighbours, the sun and the moon were gods: Shamash in Mesopotamia, Yarikh in Canaan (the Hebrew word for 'moon', yareaḥ, is the same word). Here they are given an order, like any servant. This is polemic, delivered not by a denial but by a command: the two greatest lights in the sky are told to praise YHWH.

The KJV's 'ye stars of light' is adequate, but 'all' (כָּל) belongs to the line and the actor must not drop it: there is no star that stands outside the order. 'Stars of light' is an idiom for 'shining stars': light is the stars' defining trait.

Rashi, in the packet, glosses 'stars of light' as the stars of night, and Meiri and Metzudat David read the phrase as the five visible planets; the Hebrew itself says only 'all stars of light', and I keep it general.

philological_notes.note: 'Sun'; the same consonants are the divine name Shamash in Akkadian. The word is grammatically feminine in some places, but the verb here is a plural imperative addressed to both sun and moon. The note on the sun-god is my own reading.
'Stars of light'; Rashi reads it as the stars of night, Meiri and Metzudat David as the five planets that shine more than the fixed stars.

verses.translation_literal: Praise him, heavens of the heavens, and the waters that [are] above the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him, you highest heavens, the heaven beyond heaven — and you waters held up there, above the sky itself.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the top of the ancient world picture: a vault of sky (the 'firmament' of Genesis 1) and, above that vault, a store of water held back by God's word. Rain, in this picture, comes through its windows. To an Israelite audience this was geography; the actor should say 'the waters above the heavens' as a plain fact, not as a metaphor.

'Heavens of the heavens' is the Hebrew way of making a superlative, like 'song of songs'. The KJV keeps the literal form and gets it right here; BBE's 'highest heavens' is the idea in modern dress.

The medieval commentators in the packet read the verse through their own astronomy (Radak, Meiri, Malbim all assign the heavens and the waters to specific spheres). The psalm itself has no such system: it simply stacks things, with the waters on the top step, and then brings them down: praise comes from the very top because God made all of it.

philological_notes.note: 'Heavens of the heavens', a superlative construction meaning the highest heaven. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David each place it in a different layer of the sky.
'The waters that are above the heavens': the upper waters of Genesis 1:7. Targum says they hang 'by his word', Malbim ties them to Genesis.

verses.translation_literal: Let them praise [obj] the name of YHWH, for he, he commanded, and they were created.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them all praise the name of the LORD. For he spoke the word — and they were made.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes from the second person ('praise!') to the third ('let them praise'): the poet stops calling and begins to declare, as a conductor turns from the band to the hall. The reason follows with a 'for': they praise because he commanded, and they came into being.

The Hebrew has an emphatic 'he' (הוּא) before 'commanded': 'for he — he commanded'. The KJV's 'for he commanded' drops the stress, and the actor should restore it. The verb 'were created' (נִבְרָאוּ) comes from the root used only of God's creating in the Bible (as in Genesis 1:1); the KJV keeps it, BBE's 'were made' is weaker.

Creation by command is the opposite of the way the surrounding cultures told it: in Babylon creation came by a battle with the sea, here the sea monsters of verse 7 are simply the creatures of the same word. Malbim in the packet notes that the heavens, unlike the earth, were only 'created', and Radak says the point is that only God is eternal and the rest are made.

philological_notes.note: 'He commanded'; the creating word is cast as a royal order, the same verb used for a king's decrees. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'decreed or willed'.
'They were created', passive of the verb bara, which in the Bible has God alone as its subject. Malbim distinguishes it from 'form' and 'make'.

verses.translation_literal: And he made them stand for ever, for eternity; a decree he gave, and it will not pass.
verses.translation_dramatic: He set them in their places, to stand there for ever and ever. He gave them a law, and the law will not pass away.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood moves from praise to order. 'Made them stand' (וַיַּעֲמִידֵם) is the verb of setting a post, like a guard on duty or a boundary stone: the heavenly bodies have been put in place and are not allowed to wander. 'For ever, for eternity' stacks two near-synonyms (Metzudat Zion notes the doubling of synonyms) for emphasis, and the actor should give both.

The 'decree' (חֹק) is the allotted rule, a limit or portion. Rashi reads it as the assignment of duty: this one serves by day, that one by night. In a world where the stars were the gods and could change human fate, the poem says they have been given a fixed job and cannot overstep it. The KJV 'hath made a decree' is slightly off: the verb is 'give' (נָתַן), as one gives an assignment, and the BBE 'given them their limits' is closer to the meaning.

The last word, 'pass' (יַעֲבוֹר), can also mean 'cross over', so the line can be heard as 'it will not be overstepped'. The subject is ambiguous (the decree, or the heavenly bodies themselves), and both readings fit.

philological_notes.note: 'Decree, fixed portion, limit'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a 'decree'; Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the assignment of when each light serves.
'It will pass away' or 'it will cross over / transgress'. The sentence has no stated subject, so either the decree or the bodies are meant.

verses.translation_literal: Praise [obj] YHWH from the earth, tannînim, and all deeps.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now from the earth, below: praise the LORD, you great monsters of the sea, and every deep that lies beneath the waves.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem turns the corner: after six verses of 'from the heavens', the first line of the second half repeats the opening formula and swaps one word, 'from the earth'. The mirror is deliberate, and the actor should repeat the verse 1 tone with the new place.

The first earthly voices are the creatures everyone feared. The tannînim are the great sea creatures; in Genesis 1:21 they are made on the fifth day, and elsewhere in the Bible (and in the neighbouring literature) the same word can denote the chaos-dragon, the foe of the gods. The KJV 'dragons' keeps the monster; ASV and BBE read 'sea-monsters', which is closer to the context here. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read them as large fish. Either way the point is the same: even the creatures that stood for the terror of chaos are put in the choir. 'Deeps' (תְּהֹמוֹת) is the plural of the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2.

The sea was the place Israelites feared and did not control; to name its monsters as worshippers is to tame the whole picture.

philological_notes.note: 'Sea monsters, great sea creatures'; in Genesis 1:21 the creatures of the fifth day, elsewhere also a name for chaos-monsters. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read 'big fish'; Radak ties it to Genesis 1:21.
'Deeps': the plural of tehom, the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2; Metzudat Zion glosses it as the depth of the sea.

verses.translation_literal: Fire and hail, snow and smoke, storm wind, doing his word.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fire and hail, snow and rising smoke, and the storm wind that rips across the land — all of it doing only what he says.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a list of the weather that destroyed: lightning fire, hailstones, the smoke-like vapour that rises from the ground, and the storm wind. Other peoples knew these as acts of their storm gods (Baal rode the storm in Canaanite myth), and the psalm gives the whole arsenal to YHWH. The poem does not argue the point: it simply makes them participants in the choir, each one obeying 'his word'.

The KJV's 'vapour' for קִיטוֹר is defensible: Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion all read it as the vapour that rises from the ground and looks like smoke, and Rashi gives it as 'mist' (Old French bruine). The Hebrew root is the one for smoking incense (compare the smoke of Genesis 19:28, my own cross-reference), so the literal layer says 'smoke' to keep that image, and the actor should see a column of haze rising. The KJV's 'stormy wind fulfilling his word' is correct in sense but loses the verb: the wind is 'doing' (עֹשָׂה) his word, the same verb as 'making', as if the word were a task handed down.

Rashi records a rabbinic saying (Hagigah 12b) that these were first kept in heaven, and David brought them down to earth because they are punishments and not fitting to be stored in God's own dwelling. Radak adds that the storm wind is not chance: it moves by his command, as punishment.

philological_notes.note: 'Smoke-like vapour'. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as the warm vapour rising from the ground that resembles smoke; Rashi glosses it with the Old French bruine ('mist'). The root also means 'to make smoke rise', as in incense, which is why the literal layer keeps 'smoke'.
'Doing his word': the wind carries out the command as a messenger would. Rashi reads it as 'his word and his mission'; Radak says it moves only by his order.

verses.translation_literal: The mountains and all hills; tree of fruit and all cedars.
verses.translation_dramatic: The mountains, and every hill below them; the trees that bear fruit, and the cedars, every one.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the sky and the sea, the eye now rises to the land: first the high ground, then what grows on it. 'Mountains and hills' is the standard pair for the whole contour of the country, from Hermon down to the foothills of Judah. The poem passes from stone to living wood.

The contrast in the second line is an economic one: 'fruit tree' (olive, fig, vine, pomegranate) is the tree that feeds a household, and the cedar (the great timber of Lebanon, used for temples and palaces) is the tree that builds. One feeds, one is built from. Ibn Ezra and Radak point out the second class gives no fruit, and the list therefore goes from useful to majestic. The BBE's 'all trees of the mountains' for 'cedars' is a paraphrase and not in the Hebrew.

The KJV 'fruitful trees' makes the noun a plural adjective; the Hebrew is 'tree of fruit', a collective singular, which the literal layer keeps.

philological_notes.note: 'Fruit tree', literally 'tree of fruit', a collective singular for fruit-bearing trees in general; Radak and Ibn Ezra contrast it with the cedars, which bear no fruit.
'Hills', the lower heights; Metzudat David glosses the word as the lower mountains.

verses.translation_literal: The living creature and all livestock; creeping thing and bird of wing.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wild beasts, and every herd and flock; everything that creeps on the ground, and every bird that rides the air on its wings.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem now fills the land with life. The list follows the order of creation in Genesis 1, though not in the same sequence: wild animals and domestic stock, then the small things and the birds. The word for wild animals (חַיָּה) is 'the living one', here set against 'livestock' (בְּהֵמָה): the wild and the tame. Ibn Ezra notes the same pair in Leviticus 25:7 ('for your livestock and the wild animal in your land'), where the first lives away from settlement and the second in it. Radak reads the same distinction.

The KJV 'beasts and all cattle' is acceptable. 'Creeping things' (רֶמֶשׂ) names whatever moves low along the ground: reptiles, insects, rodents, the swarm; BBE's 'insects' narrows it. 'Bird of wing' is Hebrew idiom for 'winged bird', an odd phrase that stresses the wing, and the KJV 'flying fowl' reflects it.

The animals cannot speak. Radak and Meiri both stress that the command is poetic: people are meant to hear the praise in the creatures' existence. For the stage, this is a roll-call, with each pair named and each one 'called up' before the humans.

philological_notes.note: 'Creeping thing', whatever moves low over the ground; Metzudat Zion ties the root to movement from place to place, and Radak and Metzudat David call them the small animals.
The wild animal and the domestic animal: Radak says the first is of the wilderness and the second lives in settled land; Ibn Ezra cites Leviticus 25:7 for the pair.

verses.translation_literal: Kings of earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Kings of the earth, and all the peoples they rule; princes, and every judge who sits in judgment on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now come the humans, and the order is by rank, from the top: kings, then the peoples, then the officials, then the judges. The earthly powers who sit on thrones and pass sentences are named as members of the choir, along with the sea monsters. The poem does not flatter them; it places them in a line with the hail and the cedars.

The KJV 'all people' reads as 'every person'; the Hebrew לְאֻמִּים is 'peoples, nations', plural and political. A king in the ancient Near East claimed to rule on behalf of a god, and was often addressed as a god's son; here every king of the earth is told to praise YHWH, with no mention of Israel. The word 'earth' appears twice and the second use is again 'of the earth'; the literal layer keeps both. Malbim reads kings as holders of rule and 'peoples' as holders of religion, and 'princes' and 'judges' as the next level of rule and of law.

Radak adds that the list means that every rank will praise, from the noble to the humble.

philological_notes.note: 'Peoples, nations'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'peoples'. The word is plural and political, not 'people' in the singular sense of the KJV.
'Judges of earth'; the participle of 'to judge', which in Hebrew also means to govern. Malbim reads 'princes' as rulers and 'judges' as the keepers of law and custom.

verses.translation_literal: Young men and also young women; old men with youths.
verses.translation_dramatic: Young men, and young women too; the old, with the boys beside them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last list is the whole village: the strong young men, the young women, the elders and the children at their side. It closes the downward sweep begun in verse 1: from the highest heavens to the youngest child. Each pair is matched by opposites: male and female, old and young. The 'also' (גַּם) before the young women is a small surprise that the actor should lean on; Radak reads it as saying that they too, who are busy with their own adornment, are told to give praise.

The KJV 'maidens' is a soft word for בְּתוּלוֹת, which names an unmarried young woman of marriageable age, with the status 'virgin' in the foreground; ASV has 'virgins'. 'Children' for נְעָרִים is too narrow: the word covers boys from small children to young men. The last pair uses 'with' (עִם) and not 'and': the old stand beside the young. Radak says that is because the elders teach the young how to praise, and Ibn Ezra reads the pair as one of changing strength with age.

The verse is the cue for the final call of the psalm in the next verse: all of these, together, praise the name.

philological_notes.note: 'Young women of marriageable age, virgins'; the word names a social and marital status rather than only an age.
'Old men with youths': Radak reads 'with' as the elders being beside the young to teach them to praise.

verses.translation_literal: Let them praise the name of YHWH, for exalted is his name, to him alone; his splendor is upon earth and heaven.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them all praise the name of the LORD. For his name, his alone, is lifted high, past reach, and his splendor lies over the earth and over the heavens.
verses.directors_commentary:
The long roll call of creatures ends here, and the psalm turns from naming the praisers to naming the reason. The reason is a name. In the ancient Near East a name was the presence and the reputation of a person, so to praise YHWH's name is to praise him as he is known and has acted; the verse also quietly sets it against the many divine names of the neighbors, which each belonged to a patron of a city or a force of nature. The Hebrew says this name alone is exalted (nisgav, 'set high out of reach'), and Radak notes that the verb is not said of the heavenly beings, who are already high, but of the Creator above them. Radak also reads the earthly rulers of the earlier verses as warned: their greatness passes, and only the LORD's is secure.

On the KJV: 'excellent' for nisgav is an archaism that has lost its sense; it means 'exalted' (the same root as misgav, 'a high refuge', Radak's word for the stronghold in his comment). 'Glory' for hod is acceptable but flattens it; hod is the majesty or splendor of a king's bearing, not kavod, 'weight, glory'. 'Above the earth and heaven' in the KJV can sound like a position in space; 'al is also 'over' in the sense of authority. The order, earth before heaven, reverses the opening of the psalm, which began in the heavens; Meiri thinks the earth comes first because it is the realm where his providence is most doubted, and Malbim reads it as the praise now rising from below. The accent after lebado marks a pause, so the second half, 'his splendor is over earth and heaven', should land as a separate statement.

philological_notes.note: A niphal participle, 'is set high', 'is inaccessibly exalted'. The root is used of a refuge on a height, and the sense here is that the LORD's name is both lofty and a place of safety. KJV 'excellent' obscures it.
'His splendor, majesty': the radiance that belongs to a king or a god. Metzudat David glosses it 'his majesty, fitting upon earth and heaven'. It is not the same word as kavod ('glory, weight').

Literally 'to his separateness', so 'to him alone'. In context it excludes every other name from this height; the preposition and the suffix make it an exclusive claim, not a statement about solitude.

verses.translation_literal: And he has raised a horn for his people, praise for all his faithful ones, for the sons of Israel, a people near to him. Praise Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he has lifted up a horn for his people: a cause of praise for all who are faithful to him, for the children of Israel, the people who stand close to him. Praise the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes by narrowing from the whole cosmos to one people, and the actors should feel the room tighten. The 'horn' is the horn of a wild ox or a ram, the image of strength, dignity and victory; to raise the horn is to give strength and standing (Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed for strength and rule, because those with horns grow strong when they fight). The KJV renders it 'He also exalteth the horn of his people', adding 'also' that the Hebrew lacks, and then makes the next phrase a blur: 'the praise of all his saints'. The Hebrew tehilla is 'praise' in the sense of a cause for praise, a source of renown, not the worship given by saints. 'Saints' for chasidim is the other thing to correct: these are the people of hesed, loyal covenant love, the faithful, not canonized figures. The phrase 'a people near to him' (am keravo) is the claim of intimacy. Ibn Ezra notes that am here is not in construct, and compares the construction to 'your faithful man' (ish chasidekha); the people are 'his near one'.

The tense is open. Radak takes it as the ingathering from exile, with the horn of Israel lifted above all nations; Meiri hears redemption and the choosing of a treasured people; Malbim hears Israel climbing to the head of the ladder. In performance the verb is a quiet, settled fact, since the tense is a wayyiqtol that can carry a completed act or a promise. The closing hallelu-Yah is the same word that opened the psalm, so the circle is closed and the voice should return to the pitch of the beginning.

philological_notes.note: 'Horn', the symbol of strength and honor, and by extension a ruler or a dynasty. Raising the horn means giving victory and standing. Metzudat Zion gives it as borrowed for strength and rule.

'His faithful ones', those characterized by chesed, loyal love toward God and one another. KJV 'saints' imports the later sense of the word. Ibn Ezra takes the chasidim as the faithful among Israel, not necessarily all of them.
'A people near to him', literally 'a people of his nearness' or 'his near ones'. Ibn Ezra says am is not in the construct state; the people are the ones near him.
